title: Glycogen Depletion as Metabolic Driver of Cancer Cachexia: A Mechanistic Hypothesis Linking Tumor Glucose Demand, Gluconeogenesis, and Muscle Proteolysis
content: Cancer cachexia affects 50–80% of patients with advanced malignancy and contributes to 20–30% of cancer-related deaths, yet therapies targeting the predominant cytokine-centric framework have not yielded clinically meaningful, sustained reversal. This persistent therapeutic gap suggests that an upstream driver may have been incompletely characterized. We propose a substrate-level mechanistic hierarchy: (1) the tumor Warburg phenotype, through accelerated glycolysis, with constitutive GLUT1/GLUT3-mediated insulin-independent glucose uptake, imposes a continuous and progressively escalating glucose drain on the host that scales with tumor burden and metastatic spread, as quantified by FDG-PET total lesion glycolysis; (2) host glycogen reserves (~400–500 g) are progressively depleted under this continuous demand; (3) once depleted, hepatic gluconeogenesis becomes mandatory, because even-chain fatty acids cannot generate net glucose in humans; (4) skeletal muscle proteolysis supplies the alanine and glutamine required for gluconeogenesis and TCA-cycle anaplerosis, mobilizing muscle as the only scalable gluconeogenic substrate; (5) inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β) function as downstream amplifiers of an already-engaged proteolytic program rather than as its primary drivers, consistent with the recent demonstration that cachexia proceeds in the colon carcinoma 26 model despite genetic ablation of IL-6, LIF, and IL-11.The novelty proposed here is not the recognition of tumor glucose consumption or of gluconeogenesis in cachexia, both well established, but the identification of the limited glycogen reserve, combined with the biochemical inability to derive net glucose from fat, as the substrate-level constraint that converts tumor glucose demand into mandatory proteolysis. A conceptual flux-constraint model is offered to organize the relevant variables, together with six falsifiable predictions and immediate research implications as well as clinical applications spanning glycogen monitoring as a candidate clinical biomarker and nutritional strategies oriented toward glycogen repletion.
